comments.author: scottschurr
comments.body:
I have not looked closely at this pull request.  That said, I'm not convinced that the proposed change brings enough value to justify...

1. The risk associated with the change, or
2. The costs associated with the change (review time spent, testing costs, and an additional amendment).

It looks like this change was initially intended to be part of a larger sweep of changes that @nbougalis had in mind.  Without Nik's hand on the rudder I don't foresee that larger sweep coming to fruition.  So I need to look at this proposed change in isolation.

For my eyes, at least, the risk and costs associated with this proposed change out weigh any benefits I perceive.

I'm open to being convinced otherwise.

comments.author: ckeshava
comments.body: Hello, 1. **Correctness** The documentation states that we have to use the public keys to choose a candidate for the negative UNL. But we are using the `NodeID` in such calculations [here](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/1151fba415a5949adfa1bca8bebf135355a0619c/src/ripple/app/misc/NegativeUNLVote.cpp#L149) This would entail changes to the consensus portion of the code. But in my perspective, this fixes a mistake in the code, it is not a new feature addition. Hence, an amendment should not be required, as much as an extensive code review. I'm not familiar with the amendment process. Were amendments required for bug fixes in the past? 2. **Efficiency** At the moment, we are [inter-converting](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/1151fba415a5949adfa1bca8bebf135355a0619c/src/ripple/app/misc/NegativeUNLVote.cpp#L48) between `NodeID` and `PublicKey` at every voting ledger (255th ledger). This conversion is not necessary and could be eliminated. 3. **Accuracy of documentation** I'm not convinced that the code adheres to the documentation apropos the reliability calculation. The code checks if a peer has sent a validation [here](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/1151fba415a5949adfa1bca8bebf135355a0619c/src/ripple/app/misc/NegativeUNLVote.cpp#L203). If so, the score is incremented by 1. While this ensures good network connectivity with the peer, it does not check the *behavior/non-maliciousness* of the peer. If the peer sends incorrect validations about a ledger, I believe the code would still increment the count by 1. I feel its a good change for all these reasons. @pwang200 You worked on this piece of code, I'd love to hear your opinions too

comments.author: scottschurr
comments.body:
@ckeshava, thanks for that documentation.  That helps.  And I too would appreciate hearing @pwang200's opinion regarding this change.

Regarding the three points you bring up:

1. Correctness: you are citing part of the XRPL.org documentation: https://xrpl.org/negative-unl.html#choosing-from-multiple-candidate-validators.  It seems like the easier path would be to fix that documentation.  Adding an amendment so that (working) code matches the documentation seems backwards to me.
2. Efficiency: you have a point here, that the interconversion is unnecessary.  However, does improving this particular efficiency measurably impact the efficiency of the server?  The efficiency argument should come with measurements.  There are lots of places where the server is inefficient.  We have to select places to change so that we make measurable improvements.
3. Reliability Measurement: I see you arguing that the current code does not check the...

> the *behavior/non-maliciousness* of the peer.

But it looks like this pull request does nothing to change that situation.  I don't see any changes in this pull request in `NegativeUNLVote::buildScoreTable()` to check the maliciousness of the peer more than what is currently done.  That portion of the pull request looks like it's simply switching from checking `NodeID`s to `PublicKey`s.

So to my eyes there are two good paths forward with this pull request:

1. Show numbers demonstrating that the improved efficiency from the pull request justifies the change, or
2. Close the pull request and fix the documentation so it describes the actual (current) behavior of the code.

Thoughts?  I'm still open to being convinced that this pull request has _sufficient_ merit to justify it going forward.  But I'm not convinced yet.

comments.author: ckeshava
pwang200
comments.body:
I agree with what Scott said. 

Regarding point-1, the goal is that validators can agree on the candidate if there are more than 1, assuming the validators have the same set of candidates. So what we need is a deterministic way to sort them. It doesn't matter if public key or the nodeID is used. Although inconsistent with the doc, but the code does what it should do. It is easier to change the doc. 

This will need an amendment. Because if some nodes use nodeID to sort and some nodes use public key to sort, they will pick different candidates. An amendment ensures that all nodes use the same data to sort. 

Regarding point-2, if we can avoid the inter-converting between NodeID and PublicKey, (it was not obvious to me how to avoid inter-converting 3.5 years ago, but if we can now...) that is good. But I am not sure if the performance improvement is measurable.

reviews.author: scottschurr
reviews.body:
These changes look great.  However there's still one place that squeaks a bit.

In the `SField`s the plural of `sfDisabledValidator` is spelled `sfNegativeUNL`.  That's kinda weird.  The gRPC calls the plural of `DisabledValidator` `DisabledValidators`.  That feels like the right name.

Just for comparison, in the SFields many of the plural types follow the singular/plural idiom.  Here are the ones that I've noted in the unit test I'm working on:
```
        // All of the repeated types that the test currently supports.
        static const std::map<std::string, SField const*> repeatsWhat
        {
            {sfAmendments.getName(), &sfAmendment},
            {sfHashes.getName(), &sfLedgerHash},
            {sfIndexes.getName(), &sfLedgerIndex},
            {sfMajorities.getName(), &sfMajority},
            {sfSignerEntries.getName(), &sfSignerEntry},
            {sfNegativeUNL.getName(), &sfDisabledValidator}
        };
```
Note that

- `Hashes` -> `LedgerHash` and 
- `Indexes` -> `LedgerIndex`

are already not great.  But

- `NegativeUNL` -> `DisabledValidator`

is a new level of asymmetry.

Is it too late to change `sfNegativeUNL` to `sfDisabledValidators`?

If I change here, I probably should change other places as well, which I felt confusing. I see the `disabledValidator` more as a type and `disabledValidators` as its plural (or container). And I see negativeUNL as a usage of the container. Iirc, the skip list has type hashes, but it is protocol meaning is the skip list.

reviewCommentsList.author: scottschurr
reviewCommentsList.body:
That's fine.  It's one that we can think about.  I've been thinking of the `NegativeUNL` as a heterogeneous container of three elements:

- DisabledValidators,
- ValidatorToDisable, and
- ValidatorToReEnable

This specific entry point returns only DisabledValidators.  That's why I think the rename is appropriate.  But this name doesn't leak out into the API.  So we can change it, or not, later.

comments.author: MarkusTeufelberger
comments.body: Is there a more technical description available of this, ideally including some mathematics?

comments.author: MarkusTeufelberger
comments.body:
I'm especially worried about the consensus mechanism starting to bleed into the on-ledger representation with this amendment. If servers are unreliable, a UNL registry should remove them immediately, I don't see why it would be so important to vote (some of) them out collectively after 256 ledgers and create spam objects on-ledger for everyone else. Also I don't see why this should be globally coordinated - if nodes just keep their private nUNL, the effects would be nearly the same with no need to do extra work in consensus on which widely trusted validators are globally seen as unreliable. For this reason I'd really like to see the mathematical models and proofs(!) behind this change.

If the concept itself is seen as necessary for some reason, please at least make it off-ledger. Right now everything on-ledger is agnostic to the consensus mechanism used, this somewhat "violates" the layer separation between consensus mechanism and actual database/ledger/blockchain.

comments.author: nbougalis
comments.body:
Hey @MarkusTeufelberger. First off, apologies that we didn't actually include the spec alongside the commit. It's been added with the latest commit.

>The doc links to internal data that's not published (yet?), so it is a bit hard to know why David proposed this feature the way it is designed here.

Ack, that should have been caught; apologies. The document primarily discusses the rationale for "simplifying" the original proposal by limiting the number of changes that can be done at once. Here's the relevant content:

> ### Executive Summary
> 
> The initial negative UNL specification had a lot of complexity around handling changes to the negative UNL across flag ledgers. It required some complex special cases and reduced safety significantly around flag ledgers. This updated version does not impact safety though operates a bit more slowly.
> 
>  
> ### Ledger Structures
> 
> The negative UNL contains three components. One is the current negative UNL, a list of validator public keys. The second is an entry to be added to the negative UNL on the next flag ledger. The third is an entry to be removed from the negative UNL on the next flag ledger.
> 
>  
> ### Pseudo-Transactions
> 
> A new pseudo-transaction, UNLModify, is added. It has a flag indicating whether the modification is an addition or a removal. It also has the public key of the validator to be added or removed. Like other pseudo-transactions, it has the ledger sequence number to ensure its ID is unique.
> 
> A UNLModify/add transaction sets the validator to be added at the next flag ledger, overwriting a previous entry (if any). A UNLModify/remove transaction sets the validator to be removed at the next flag ledger, overwriting a previous entry (if any). Note that an add for a validator already in the UNL or a remove for a valdiator not in the UNL is a no-op and does not modify the ledger.
> 
>  
> ### Flag Ledger Logic
> 
> When deciding how to vote in a flag ledger, each server will take the negative UNL from preceding ledger, apply any addition or removal specified in the ledger, and then decide how to choose a server to add and a server to remove from the negative UNL.
> 
> A validator is chosen to vote to remove from the negative UNL as follows:
> 
> 1. The server looks for any validators on the negative UNL that produced validations for the ledger prior to this flag ledger.
> 2. If none are found, this server will not vote to remove an entry.
> 3. If any are found, the public key is XORed with the hash of the parent ledger and the one with the lowest XOR result is chosen.
> 
> A validator is chosen to vote to add to the negative UNL as follows:
> 
> 1. The server looks for any validators not on the negative UNL that have not produced any recent valid validations.
> 2. If none are found, this server will not vote to add an entry.
> 3. If any are found, the public key is XORed with the hash of the parent ledger and the one with the lowest XOR result is chosen.
> 
> Before a ledger after a flag ledger’s transactions are executed, the UNL is modified by the add and remove entries in the ledger, if any, and the add/remove entries are removed.
> 
>  
> ### Ledger Validation Logic
> 
> There is a three step process to determining what UNL to use when fully-validating a ledger. First, the server must decide what negative UNL to use. Second, the server must combine the negative UNL with its own UNL and determine what the effective UNL and quorum requirement is for that ledger. Lastly, the server must see if it has sufficient validations.
> 
> My current recommendation for step one is to simply use the UNL in the ledger. Because at least 60% of the server’s own local UNL is always required to accept a ledger as fully validated, I do not believe it is necessary to confirm that the negative UNL is not too different from that of prior ledgers to protect against malicious validators.
> 
> The quorum logic is as follows:
> 
> 1. Only validations from validators that are on your local UNL but not on the negative UNL count.
> 
> 2. Compute 60% of the number validators on your local UNL (round up).
> 
> 3. Compute 80% of the validators on our local UNL that are not on the negative UNL (round up).
> 
> 4. The effective quorum requirement is the greater of the numbers you computed in steps 2 and 3.
> 
> For example, say there are 32 validators on your UNL, 8 entries on the negative UNL of which 7 are on your UNL. The only validations you count are any from the 32-7 validators on your UNL and not on the negative UNL. So there are 25 candidate validators. The quroum is the greater of 60% of 32 and 80% of 25, both of which are 20. So the required quorum is 20 of 25.

Now, you wrote:

>I'm especially worried about the consensus mechanism starting to bleed into the on-ledger representation with this amendment. _If servers are unreliable, a UNL registry should remove them immediately_

This is certainly reasonable and arguably should be done by all responsible publishers. But no publisher can react in near real-time and the reality is that sometimes servers go down for more than just a couple of minutes and that's not necessarily an indication of unreliability. It's reasonable for a UNL publisher to have a policy that, e.g. an outage exceeding 24 hours triggers removal. But what to do during those 24 hours? 

This change aims to target that "window" of time between a validator experiencing an outage and the UNL publisher responding by removing that validtor.

We've previously discussed using the ledger for storing such objects, most recently in a conversation involving storing of manifests. You had similar objections back then and I do agree that they are legitimate and certainly merit consideration. With that said, I'm not sure that I agree that this is an inappropriate usage of the ledger or that the consensus is "bleeding into the on-ledger representation."

I'll follow up on some of your other questions tomorrow. :vulcan_salute:

comments.author: pwang200
comments.body:
@MarkusTeufelberger "why this has to be coordinated through a (voted + recorded) pseudo transaction instead of decided privately by each server instead"
Sorry for the late reply. This is what I think: the voted + recorded approach has two desired properties. First, the negative UNL on the ledger is agreed by the network. As a result, the UNLs of nodes are affected the same way. Hence we don't hurt the UNL overlapping condition in the network. If nodes decide privately, they could disable different validators, that leads to reduced UNL overlapping, which lowers the network safety. Secondly, a ledger can be considered as a synchronization point (or a discrete logical clock time), an on ledger negative UNL will take effect at the same logical clock time. In other word, with an on ledger negative UNL, nodes will use the same negative UNL at the same time.

comments.author: MarkusTeufelberger
comments.body:
As long as UNLs mostly overlap, removing nodes wouldn't necessarily reduce that overlap. It can also increase it. Also network safety isn't reduced in any way (recorded+ coordinated, private + coordinated or private + uncoordinated implementation), only network liveness.

I already suggested using flag ledgers as synchronization points, there's no need to synchronize with others though. A node could just update its nUNL without consulting others at every 256th ledger (which happens to be coordinated with others anyways, so all nUNLs network wide get updated at the same time - they would just look potentially different, e.g. in case some node has severe routing problems to parts of the network).

I get that with an on-ledger implementation they would all be using the same one - but since 80% of nodes would even need to agree that these nodes are unreliable, this would only capture nodes that have (from a network POV) a catastrophic failure, like being offline or extremely overloaded. If a node on my UNL is "reliably unreliable" for me, it should be put on my nUNL - irrespective of if it is unreliable for someone else. Also I don't see why other nodes should be able to force my node to remove a (from my node's PoV) perfectly fine validating node from its UNL.

Lastly, this leaks out UNL information from validators (as I understand it, a validator would only try to vote out nodes that it has on its private UNL). A possible attack(?) scenario would be to run a validator and switch it off for ~130 ledgers to see which other validators want to vote it out. That way I can know with certainty how widely trusted my validator is across the network, even if these votes never make it into a validated ledger (in case my validator doesn't yet have "UNL dominance", meaning it is on 80+% of UNLs of other "UNL dominant" nodes).

comments.author: pwang200
comments.body: I share your concerns. But without on-ledger negative UNL, if nodes disable validators privately, I cannot see if it's safe. It will be like simply lower the quorum from 80% to a lower percentage (with a delay due to flag ledgers).

comments.author: movitto
comments.body:
I find this feature fascinating though am no expert on Byzantine Consensus so can't comment too much on the theory behind the implementation. A couple things to note though

- This introduces a 'quasi' on-ledger UNL management mechanism, where nodes are responsible for constructing the list privately off ledger, but UNL entries may be added/removed via an on-ledger mechanism. Obviously there are tradeoffs here but this does result in an inconsistency in UNL management which raises some flags. Would it be possible to extend the concept presented here further and allow nodes to recommend validators to be included in the UNL for non-performance reasons? (expanded my datacenter, recommend a new node spun up in a geographically disparate location, etc)

- Looking at the code it seems 50% missed validation is the cutoff point, the "low water mark" to determine when a validator is unreliable. I'm curious as to how this figure was derived? Was it through analysis of the network or did it just seem like a good number? If a node is only keeping up with 55% of validations they would still be considered a reliable node. Perhaps the low / high water marks can be voted on as well depending on the performance of the network.

- Consider calling this feature 'UNL Blacklist' (or perhaps UNBL - Unique Node BlackList) as this would more accurately describe what is actually occurring when certain validators are added to a list to ignore

comments.author: pwang200
comments.body:
@movitto 
-- I realized the inconsistency in UNL management as well. Extending the concept to recommend validators is an interesting idea. That leads me thinking about David's Two-layer Consensus post. I personally think recommending validators of the lower layer could be one of the responsibilities of the top layer (or the governing layer). 

-- Yes, so far "it just seems like a good number". I acknowledge the need for analysis of the network. It has not been a priority yet. A targeted scenario of the negative UNL, and an important one, is like several validators go offline during a long weekend. In these kinds of cases, 50% seems a good number. Of course, 60% may seem good too. I will collect data and do some analysis. Though I am not sure if the extra complexity of voting on the water marks are needed. 

-- I feel the word "blacklist" might be misleading. A modification of the original UNL changes two things: who to trust, and who contribute to quorum number calculation and count towards full validation of ledgers. Negative UNL does not change who to trust. So I feel "Blacklist" is kind of too strong. The "global Synchronized Health check Interval Transgressor list" might be more accurate. :-) As @MarkusTeufelberger said.

> It is extremely important to keep in mind that this doesn't change the consensus logic or which validators vote on which transactions to include in a ledger. It only affects a server's local decision of when to consider a ledger validated. **Being on this list in no way affects a server's ability to contribute to the network's censorship resistance.**

How does this work if the following is true?

> The quorum logic is as follows:
> 1. Only validations from validators that are on your local UNL but not on the negative UNL count.

As long as you are on someone's Synchronized Healthcheck Interval Transgressor list, they will treat your validations as noise, if I understand this correctly and not just lower their Quorum by the number of validators on the list (so if someone on the list manages to validate again, their votes count).

Also I'd STILL like to explore/discuss the possibility of doing this locally on nodes without putting metadata on the ledger and voting upon it. Forcing someone off everyone's UNL (is this even actually possible to enforce/detect?) even if they are potentially working just fine is not something that should be considered lightly. Also increasing RAM usage on every node (not just validator) out there (even slightly) just for something that potentially can't even be enforced. As I understand it, all I need to do after this amendment passes (because `rippled` by default votes for it and nobody changes defaults) is to patch out the respective sections in the code, recompile, and my validator will happily vote others in or out, yet completely ignore the nUNL in actual Consensus. Maybe this just should be a config setting anyways ("enable_nUNL").

prs.body:
The Negative UNL is a protocol change to improve the network’s reliability in the face of failed validators without sacrificing network safety. The Negative UNL protocol uses the existing consensus algorithm for the network to agree on a list of validators that are believed to be unreliable at the moment and lists the validators on the ledgers. If a validator V is on that list, it would still participate in consensus in precisely the same way. But nodes with V in their UNL adjust the quorum and V’s validation message is not counted when verifying if a ledger is fully validated. When V becomes reliable, nodes use the consensus algorithm to vote it off the list.

This feature adds a new pseudo-transaction type and a Negative UNL component to the ledger data structure. Any tools or systems that rely on the format of this data will have to be updated.

This feature will need an amendment to activate.

reviews.author: carlhua
reviews.body: Good stuff @pwang200  I left some comments and I have one major comment that I would like to ask you to consider. The implementation as it stands performs bulk of the calculation at a single synchronization point - which is at a flag ledger. This increases the node's workload at every 256 ledger. Depending on the amount of work, we can potentially see a jitter in the network due to a spike in work load. Although I doubt its "that much" work, we should generally try to avoid doing lots of work at any single one point. Instead, its good practice to distribute the work over a period of time "naturally". In this case, I would ask to do the actual accumulation of scores and other housekeeping over every ledger and only at flag ledger we would do a determination. I would imagine going forward, as the software evolves only more work would be done at flag ledger and its always good to not overload the amount of work needed at any one concentrated point.

reviewCommentsList.author: nbougalis
reviewCommentsList.body:
I agree that sticking to integer arithmetic works; we can always write `INT * FLOAT` as `INT * INT / INT` for almost every `FLOAT` value we care about here:

| Floating Expression | Equivalent Integer |
|:------------------:|:-------------------------:|
|`256 * 0.5` | `256 * / 2` |
|`256 * 0.8` | `(256 * 4) / 5` |
|`256 * 0.9` | `(256 * 9) / 10` |

I don't _think_ the C++ standard actually mandates IEEE floating-point math⁠ but I don't think that generally "bites" us for the numbers we're using—perhaps @HowardHinnant or @scottschurr can correct me. If it does, then we should use the floating point arithmetic format, since it's "easier" to read: I understand *`0.8`* as "80% percent" without having to think. I don't have the same "intuitive" response to *`4 / 5`*. 

As a sidenote, and only because of the specific numbers involved, we should consider moving away from duocentehexaquinquagesimal… there's really not much point in it, and using decimal here makes a lot more sense, especially since we're talking percentages and those are best expressed in that base.

I'd like to do that across the codebase (consensus, amendment voting, etc) but a new feature seems like a good place to start.
